extracted.intended_audience: practitioners (attorneys) who represent trademark applicants before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing the ethical and regulatory conduct of practitioners (U.S. attorneys) representing trademark applicants before the United States Patent and Trademark Office, including signature and representation rules, duties of competence/diligence/communication, specimen review expectations, and disciplinary/sanctioning procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney for Foreign Trademark Applicants (U.S. Counsel Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants, registrants, or parties to a trademark proceeding whose domicile is not located within the U.S. or its territories must be represented by an attorney who is an active member in good standing of the bar of the highest court of a state in the U.S. (see Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney for Foreign Trademark Applicants and Registrants, 84 FR 31498; 37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. Counsel Rule became effective August 3, 2019. It is intended to increase USPTO customer compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations, improve accuracy of submissions, and safeguard the integrity of the U.S. trademark register. Practitioners representing foreign-domiciled applicants are expected to be reasonably well informed about the rule and to ensure compliance (e.g., bona fide specimen review).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Signature Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory; a person electronically signing a document must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature placed between two forward slash ('/') symbols in the electronic submission (see 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a) and (c) and 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP guidance: 'All documents must be personally signed... The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory.' Typing someone else's electronic signature is not a valid signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness of Declarations and Accuracy of Specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications contain declarations signed under penalty of perjury; signatories make specific representations regarding use of the mark in commerce and/or intent to use the mark in commerce, and false statements are subject to punishment under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO relies on such declarations when examining applications and issuing registrations. Practitioners must ensure specimens and declarations accurately reflect actual use; filing materially altered or mocked-up specimens or false declarations undermines register integrity and risks invalid registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner Competency (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client (37 C.F.R. § 11.101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent representation includes familiarizing oneself with applicable rules (e.g., U.S. Counsel Rule, USPTO trademark rules and regulations) so that filings and conduct comply with those requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Diligence and Promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client (37 C.F.R. § 11.103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires taking reasonable steps to ensure trademark filings are filed in accordance with the U.S. Counsel Rule and USPTO trademark rules and regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications with Client — Informing of Consequences (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must communicate with clients, including informing them of actual or potential adverse consequences so clients can make informed decisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a) and (b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to inform clients about noncompliance with the U.S. Counsel Rule or defective filings may violate this duty and deprive clients of making informed choices about their applications/registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct Prejudicial to the Integrity of the Trademark Registration System (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice, including failing to take reasonable steps to ensure trademark documents (including declarations) filed with the USPTO were signed by the named signatory and adequately reviewed prior to signing (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing impermissible signatures or insufficient review of specimens/declarations can adversely affect the integrity of the federal trademark registration process and may render resulting registrations potentially invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Conduct Adversely Reflecting on Fitness to Practice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in other conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before entering business relationships with third parties (e.g., foreign intermediaries), practitioners must make reasonable inquiries whether and how the third party will communicate with applicants and sign/file trademark applications; failure to do so can violate this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Know Identity of the Client and to Avoid Foreseeable Prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: A USPTO practitioner has an ethical obligation to know the identity of the client and how signatures may be entered when filing documents before the Office; practitioners are expected to take reasonable steps to avoid foreseeable prejudice to client rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with a foreign intermediary, the client remains the trademark applicant/owner. Receiving instructions via an intermediary does not change client identity, and practitioners must ensure steps are taken to protect client interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bona Fide Review of Specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who represent trademark applicants before the USPTO are expected to undertake a bona fide review of specimens submitted in support of an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. Counsel Rule and related guidance emphasize that practitioners should ensure specimens genuinely show use in commerce and are not mocked-up or digitally altered; failure to review specimens can contribute to inaccurate or fraudulent submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to Provide Bar Information When Representing Applicants/Registrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified U.S. attorneys are required to provide their bar information when representing applicants and registrants, whether domiciled inside or outside the U.S. (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.17(b)(3), 2.32(a)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing accurate bar information helps ensure proper accountability and transparency in representation before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Reliance on Filings and Risk of Invalid Registrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO relies on declarations and filings when examining and issuing registrations; filings signed by an unauthorized signatory or containing false statements can lead to invalid registrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must ensure authenticity and authority of signatures and accuracy of filings because such errors undermine the trademark register's integrity and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation to Terminate or Correct Relationships that Produce Noncompliant Filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who become aware that a third party (e.g., foreign intermediary) is causing improper filings (e.g., altered specimens, improper signatures) are expected to take corrective action, including terminating relationships if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions can include notifying USPTO, informing clients, implementing specimen review/approval protocols, and ceasing to act where noncompliance continues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Prior Disciplinary Records as Aggravating Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may consider the record of a disciplinary proceeding, including the Final Order, when addressing further complaints of similar misconduct and may use it (i) as an aggravating factor in determining discipline and/or (ii) to rebut statements by or on respondent's behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner’s prior discipline can influence future sanction severity and can be cited in subsequent proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and Probationary Obligations (as imposed in this Final Order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreed sanctions include public reprimand, placement on probation for twelve months, mandated continuing legal education (six hours: two on ethics/professional responsibility, four on trademark law), thorough review of TMEP and 37 C.F.R. § 2.11 and related commentary, weekly TESS searches for cases naming the practitioner, prompt notification to USPTO of unauthorized filings, and quarterly written reports to OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noncompliance with probation conditions may prompt an Order to Show Cause and potential immediate suspension for up to nine months; the OED Director may seek discrete discipline for misconduct forming the basis for an Order to Show Cause. The Final Order will be published in OED's FOIA Reading Room and the Official Gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural Rule: Personal Entry of Electronic Signature in TEAS Forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must personally enter their electronic signature in TEAS forms (direct or emailed keystroke entry) and may not allow another person to enter their signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of familiarity with TEAS signature requirements is not a defense; practitioners are expected to understand electronic-signature mechanics and ensure compliance before filing.
